2013A16.goal: A triangle and its mirror image in the line $x=8$ overlap. We want the area of their union: twice one triangle minus the overlap.

tools.name: Shoelace formula
tools.why: Area from coordinates.

tools.name: Union of two regions
tools.why: The overlap is counted twice in $[A]+[B]$.

tools.name: Reflection in $x=8$
tools.why: Distances to the line are preserved.

2013A16.approach: Compute the triangle's area. Reflect the vertices. Notice two sides of the original lie along sides of the image (same slopes through $(8,-3)$), so the overlap is a kite symmetric about $x=8$.

steps.title: The overlap
steps.explain: The image has vertices $(10,5),(8,-3),(7,1)$. Side $(8,-3)$–$(9,1)$ of the original lies on the image's side $(8,-3)$–$(10,5)$ (both slope $4$), and similarly on the left. Sides $(6,5)$–$(9,1)$ and $(10,5)$–$(7,1)$ cross at $(8,\tfrac73)$. Overlap: kite $(8,-3),(9,1),(8,\tfrac73),(7,1)$ with diagonals $\tfrac{16}3$ and $2$: area $\tfrac{16}3$.

check.q: A kite has diagonals $\tfrac{16}3$ and $2$. Its area?

2013A16.bridge: Find the area, the overlap kite, and subtract.
solution: The overlap is the kite $(8,-3),(9,1),(8,\tfrac73),(7,1)$ with area $\tfrac{16}3$.
2013A16.shortcut: Symmetry about $x=8$ means the overlap is symmetric; compute half and double.
traps: Assuming the overlap is a triangle.
2013A16.recognize: A shape and its reflection: union $=2\times$ area $-$ overlap; the overlap is symmetric about the mirror line.

2013A17.goal: Friends visit every $3$, $4$, $5$ days, all together yesterday. We count days in the next $365$ with exactly two visitors. The pattern repeats every $\operatorname{lcm}(3,4,5)=60$ days.

tools.name: Common multiples
tools.why: A day is a multiple of both periods.

tools.name: Exactly two
tools.why: All-three days are counted in each of the three pairs.

2013A17.approach: In one $60$-day cycle count days that are multiples of $12$, $15$, $20$, and subtract the all-three day ($60$) from each. Then handle $365=6\cdot60+5$.

steps.title: One cycle
steps.explain: Multiples in $1..60$: of $12$: $5$; of $15$: $4$; of $20$: $3$. Each includes day $60$ (all three). Exactly two: $(5-1)+(4-1)+(3-1)=9$.

check.q: How many multiples of $15$ are in $1..60$?

steps.title: Whole period
steps.explain: $6$ full cycles give $54$. The last $5$ days (days $361$–$365$, i.e. $1$–$5$ mod $60$) contain none. Total $54$.

2013A17.bridge: Count exactly-two days in one $60$-day cycle and scale.
solution: Per cycle: $4+3+2=9$ days with exactly two visitors.
2013A17.shortcut: Exactly-two days are pair-lcm multiples that are not multiples of $60$.
traps: Forgetting to remove the all-three days.
2013A17.recognize: Periodic events: find the lcm period, count one period with inclusion–exclusion, then scale.

2013A18.goal: A line through $A$ splits quadrilateral $ABCD$ into equal areas and meets $CD$ at $P$. We want $P$. Triangle $APD$ must have half the area.

tools.name: Shoelace formula
tools.why: Area from coordinates.

tools.name: Triangle on the $x$-axis
tools.why: $A$ and $D$ lie on the $x$-axis, so the height is $P$'s $y$-coordinate.

2013A18.approach: Find $[ABCD]=\tfrac{15}2$. The piece $APD$ is a triangle with base $AD=4$ on the $x$-axis, so its area is $2y_P$. Set $2y_P=\tfrac{15}4$, then find $x_P$ on line $CD$.
2013A18.bridge: Get the total area, use $[APD]=2y_P$, and locate $P$ on $CD$.
2013A18.shortcut: Choose the piece that is a triangle with a base on an axis; its area is one coordinate times a constant.
traps: Using the other piece (quadrilateral $ABCP$), which is harder.
2013A18.recognize: Area-bisecting lines from a vertex: make one piece a triangle with an easy base and solve for the height.

2013A19.goal: For how many bases $b$ does $2013$ end in digit $3$? The last digit in base $b$ is the remainder mod $b$.

tools.name: Last digit = remainder
tools.why: $n=b\cdot q+r$ with $0\le r<b$.

2013A19.approach: $2013\bmod b=3$ means $b\mid2010$ and $b>3$ (the digit $3$ must be allowed). Count divisors of $2010$ greater than $3$.

check.q: In base $7$, what is the last digit of $45$?

solution: $2013$ ends in $3$ in base $b$ iff $b\mid2010$ and $b>3$.
2013A19.shortcut: "Ends in digit $d$ in base $b$" $\iff b\mid n-d$ and $b>d$.
2013A19.recognize: Last digits in other bases are remainders; count divisors of $n-d$.

2013A20.goal: A unit square rotates $45^\circ$ about its centre. We want the area of all points it passes over. Split by direction from the centre: in some directions the farthest point is a moving corner (a circular arc), in others a side of the start or end square.

tools.name: Corner path
tools.why: Distance from centre to a corner of a unit square.

tools.name: Sector area
tools.why: Fraction of a disc.

tools.name: $	an22.5^circ$
tools.why: Half-angle formula.

2013A20.approach: Work in one quarter (by $90^\circ$ symmetry). Directions from $45^\circ$ to $90^\circ$ are reached by a moving corner, giving a $45^\circ$ sector. Directions from $0^\circ$ to $45^\circ$ are bounded by the start or end square's side, giving two thin triangles.

steps.title: The corner sector
steps.explain: A corner starts at angle $45^\circ$ and moves to $90^\circ$ at distance $\tfrac{\sqrt2}2$. That sweeps a sector of area $\tfrac18\pi\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac{\pi}{16}$.

steps.title: The two triangles
steps.explain: For directions $22.5^\circ$–$45^\circ$ the original square's side $x=\tfrac12$ is farthest; for $0^\circ$–$22.5^\circ$ the final square's side is. Each gives a triangle with legs $\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac12(1-\tan22.5^\circ)=\tfrac{2-\sqrt2}{2}$: area $\tfrac{2-\sqrt2}{8}$.

2013A20.bridge: Divide one quarter into a corner sector and two side triangles, then multiply by $4$.
solution: In each quarter, a corner sweeps a $45^\circ$ sector of radius $\tfrac{\sqrt2}2$: $\tfrac\pi{16}$.
The rest of the quarter is two triangles bounded by the start and end squares' sides: $2\cdot\tfrac{2-\sqrt2}8$.
2013A20.shortcut: Swept region = union of start and end squares plus the four corner "caps" between arcs and the star's points.
traps: Using only the union of the start and end squares.
Using a full quarter circle for each corner.
2013A20.recognize: Regions swept by rotating shapes: split by direction; corners trace arcs, sides give straight boundaries.

2013A21.goal: Pirate $k$ takes $\tfrac k{12}$ of what remains. With the smallest starting amount giving whole shares, we want the $12$th pirate's share. Track what remains as a product of fractions.

tools.name: Remainder after $k$ pirates
tools.why: Each pirate leaves $\tfrac{12-k}{12}$ of the remainder.

tools.name: Prime powers
tools.why: Needed to clear denominators.

2013A21.approach: The last pirate gets $R_{11}=N\cdot\tfrac{11!}{12^{11}}$. For this to be a whole number, $N$ must be a multiple of $\tfrac{12^{11}}{\gcd(12^{11},11!)}=2^{14}3^7$. Check earlier shares are whole for this $N$; then compute $R_{11}$.

check.q: After pirate $1$ takes $\tfrac1{12}$, what fraction remains?

steps.title: Smallest $N$
steps.explain: $\tfrac{12^{11}}{11!}$ in lowest terms has denominator part $2^{22-8}3^{11-4}=2^{14}3^7$. So $N=2^{14}3^7$; one can check all earlier remainders are whole too.

check.q: How many factors of $2$ are in $11!$?

2013A21.bridge: Write the last share as $N\cdot\tfrac{11!}{12^{11}}$, choose the smallest $N$, and simplify.
solution: The smallest $N$ making every share whole is $2^{14}3^7$.
2013A21.shortcut: The answer is the part of $11!$ not divisible by $2$ or $3$: $5^2\cdot7\cdot11$.
traps: Forgetting to cancel the $2$s and $3$s in $11!$.
2013A21.recognize: Successive fractional shares: the remainder is a product of fractions; integrality means clearing a fixed denominator.

2013A22.goal: Six unit spheres sit at the vertices of a hexagon of side $2$, inside a big sphere centred at the hexagon's centre. An eighth sphere touches all six and the big sphere. We find its radius.

tools.name: Tangent spheres
tools.why: Centres and the point of tangency are collinear.

tools.name: Regular hexagon
tools.why: It is made of equilateral triangles.

2013A22.approach: The big sphere has radius $2+1=3$. The eighth sphere's centre lies on the axis through the centre, at height $h$. Tangency to a small sphere: $\sqrt{4+h^2}=r+1$; to the big sphere: $h+r=3$.

steps.title: Big sphere
steps.explain: Small centres are $2$ from the middle; internal tangency gives $R=2+1=3$.

check.q: What is the distance from a regular hexagon's centre to a vertex if the side is $2$?

2013A22.bridge: Use one tangency for height and another for distance to a small centre.
solution: The eighth centre is at height $h=3-r$ on the axis, with $\sqrt{4+h^2}=r+1$.
2013A22.shortcut: Set up a right triangle: horizontal $2$, vertical $3-r$, hypotenuse $r+1$.
traps: Placing the eighth sphere in the hexagon's plane.
Using internal tangency with the small spheres.
2013A22.recognize: Mutually tangent spheres with symmetry: put the unknown centre on the axis and use two tangency equations.

2013A23.goal: The circle centred at $A$ through $B$ meets $BC$ again at $X$; $BX$ and $CX$ are integers. We want $BC$. Power of the point $C$ gives a product equal to a fixed number.

tools.name: Power of a point
tools.why: For a point outside a circle, the product of distances to the two intersections on any line is constant.

tools.name: Triangle inequality
tools.why: Sides of a genuine triangle.

2013A23.approach: Power of $C$: $CX\cdot CB=97^2-86^2=11\cdot183=2013$. So $CX$ and $CB$ are complementary factors of $2013=3\cdot11\cdot61$. Pick the pair satisfying the triangle inequality.

check.q: Which of $2013,671,183,61$ is strictly between $11$ and $183$?

2013A23.bridge: Use power of the point $C$ and the triangle inequality.
2013A23.recognize: A circle centred at a vertex through another vertex: power of a point from the third vertex.

2013A24.goal: Each of $3$ Central players plays each of $3$ Northern players twice, in $6$ rounds of $3$ simultaneous games. Each round pairs the players up, which is a permutation of $3$. We count schedules.

tools.name: Rounds as permutations
tools.why: Each Central player faces exactly one Northern player per round.

tools.name: Two families
tools.why: Within each family, every Central–Northern pair occurs exactly once.

tools.name: Multiset arrangements
tools.why: Three rounds each used twice.

2013A24.approach: Every pair (Central $i$, Northern $j$) is covered by exactly one even and one odd permutation. If even ones are used $e_1,e_2,e_3$ times and odd ones $o_1,o_2,o_3$ times, each pair needs $e_a+o_b=2$ for all $a,b$. That forces all $e$ equal and all $o$ equal: $(1,1)$, $(2,0)$ or $(0,2)$.

steps.title: The counting equations
steps.explain: Each pair is in one even and one odd permutation, and every combination of an even and an odd permutation shares exactly one pair. So $e_a+o_b=2$ for every $a,b$, forcing $e_1=e_2=e_3=e$ and $o_1=o_2=o_3=o$ with $e+o=2$.

check.q: If $e_a+o_b=2$ for all $a,b$, must all $e_a$ be equal?

steps.title: Count each case
steps.explain: $e=o=1$: all six permutations once each, in any order: $6!=720$. $e=2,o=0$: three rounds each twice: $\tfrac{6!}{2!2!2!}=90$; same for $e=0,o=2$: $90$.

2013A24.bridge: Model rounds as permutations, use the two families, and count arrangements.
solution: Each round is a permutation of $3$; pairs are covered once by each family (even, odd).
Covering each pair exactly twice forces equal use within families: $(1,1)$, $(2,0)$ or $(0,2)$.
2013A24.shortcut: Latin squares: the even and odd permutations of $3$ each form one.
traps: Counting only the case using all six permutations ($720$).
2013A24.recognize: Round-robin scheduling between two teams: rounds are permutations; coverage conditions give equations on usage counts.

2013A25.goal: All $20$ diagonals of a regular octagon are drawn. We count interior points where two or more meet. Generic counting gives one point per choice of $4$ vertices, but regular octagons have points where three or four diagonals meet, which are over-counted.

tools.name: Quadruples give crossings
tools.why: Each $4$ vertices form a convex quadrilateral whose diagonals cross once.

tools.name: Correcting for concurrency
tools.fact: \text{a point where }m\text{ diagonals meet is counted }\binom m2\text{ times}
tools.why: Each pair of those diagonals comes from a quadruple.

2013A25.approach: Start with $70$. The centre has $4$ long diagonals meeting, counted $\binom42=6$ times instead of once: subtract $5$. There are $8$ points, arranged symmetrically around the centre, where exactly $3$ diagonals meet; each is counted $3$ times instead of once: subtract $16$.

steps.title: Generic count
steps.explain: Any $4$ vertices form a quadrilateral whose two diagonals cross inside: $\binom84=70$ crossings counted with multiplicity.

steps.title: The centre
steps.explain: The $4$ long diagonals all pass through the centre: $\binom42=6$ counts for $1$ point. Subtract $5$.

check.q: How many pairs among $4$ concurrent lines?

steps.title: Triple points
steps.explain: By the octagon's symmetry there are $8$ interior points where exactly three diagonals meet; each is counted $3$ times instead of once. Subtract $16$. Total $70-5-16=49$.

2013A25.bridge: Count quadruples, then correct for the centre and the triple points.
solution: Each $4$-vertex set gives one crossing: $70$ with multiplicity.
The centre (4 diagonals) is counted $6$ times: subtract $5$.
The $8$ triple points are counted $3$ times each: subtract $16$.
2013A25.shortcut: For regular polygons, always look for concurrency at the centre and at symmetric interior points.
2013A25.recognize: Counting diagonal intersections: $\binom n4$ for general position, then correct for concurrent diagonals in regular polygons.
